# Chapter 5 — The Typed Five-Class Drift Taxonomy

::: {.callout-note}
## In this chapter
A deterministic substrate that is correct on the day it is stamped and never checked again is a snapshot, not a substrate. The fourth differentiated capability is what keeps the first three true over time: a typed drift engine that validates every facet on every principal and sorts each divergence into one of five named classes, each with a severity and a remediation policy. This chapter walks the five classes, explains why typing the drift is what makes it actionable, and why dry-run and halt-on-critical defaults make the engine safe to run continuously. The normative contracts are `ADR-040` and `ADR-012`; the customer-facing walk-through is the [Drift Walk-through](/customer-documents/reference-architecture/drift-walkthrough.html).
:::

## Why Drift Is the Real Adversary

Stamping an organization's structure correctly is the easy part. Keeping it correct is the hard part, and it is where most attempts at an organizational substrate quietly fail. People change departments. Divisions are renamed. Cost centers are retired. Devices are reassigned. An HR feed hiccups and writes a malformed date. A well-meaning administrator edits an attribute by hand. None of these is dramatic, and that is exactly the danger: organizational structure does not break loudly, it erodes silently, and a substrate that is not continuously reconciled is correct only on the day it was built.

The IGA platforms and Microsoft's primitives have monitoring, but not of this. They watch for access anomalies, certification overdue dates, and policy violations. What they do not watch is whether the organizational structure underneath those controls still matches what it is supposed to be — because, as the earlier chapters established, they do not own that structure as a validated substrate in the first place. You cannot detect drift in a thing you never defined as canonical.

> Organizational structure does not fail; it erodes. A substrate without continuous reconciliation is a photograph of the org chart on the day it was taken, growing less true with every reorganization, transfer, and stray keystroke.

## Five Classes, Each Named

OrgPath's drift engine reconciles the live tenant state against canon by validating every facet on every principal — and the decisive design choice is that it does not report drift as a single undifferentiated alarm. It *types* each divergence into one of five named classes, because what broke determines who should fix it and how.

**Format** drift is a typed facet whose value fails its pattern — a hire date in US format where ISO is required. It is high severity and never auto-fixed, because a malformed date usually signals an upstream script writing bad data, and the fix is to debug the script, not to paper over its output.

**Value** drift is an enumerated facet carrying a value that is not in its enumeration at all — a department that does not exist in the codebook. It is medium severity. Where the HR source is authoritative, the correct value can be written back; for principals not driven by HR, the finding flags for human review.

**Slot** drift is a codebook-integrity problem: two facets bound to the same attribute slot, or a slot rebound without a governing decision. It is high severity and never auto-fixed, because it is not a data error on a principal but a defect in the canon itself, and only a governance action can resolve it.

**Orphan** drift is an enumeration value with zero matching principals — a department in the codebook that nobody is in. It is low severity and flag-only, because the empty value might be a placeholder for an expected hire or a planned reorganization, and deleting it requires a reviewed change rather than an automatic sweep.

**Phantom** drift is the inverse: a principal still carrying a value the codebook has deprecated. It is low severity, and when the deprecated value has a recorded successor, the principal can be reassigned to it; when it does not, the finding flags for manual reassignment.

| Class | What diverged | Severity | Auto-fix posture |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Format** | A typed facet fails its pattern | High (P1) | Never — debug the upstream source |
| **Value** | An enumerated facet's value is unknown | Medium (P2) | Sometimes — write back from HR when authoritative |
| **Slot** | Codebook integrity: collided or rebound slot | High (P1) | Never — requires a governance action |
| **Orphan** | An enumeration value with no principals | Low (P3) | Flag only — may be a deliberate placeholder |
| **Phantom** | A principal carries a deprecated value | Low (P3) | Reassign when a successor is recorded |

## Why Typing the Drift Is the Capability

It would be possible to detect all of these and report them as one stream of "problems." That is roughly what generic configuration-monitoring tools do, and it is why their output is so often ignored: an undifferentiated list of findings, all looking equally urgent, routes nowhere in particular and overwhelms whoever has to triage it.

Typing the drift is what converts detection into action. Because each finding carries a class, a severity, and a facet, it routes to the right place automatically. A Format failure goes to whoever owns the upstream feed, urgently, because something is writing bad data right now. A Slot collision goes to governance, because canon itself is wrong. An Orphan goes into a low-priority digest, because it is probably fine. The finding names the exact facet and slot on the exact principal, so the person who receives it does not have to investigate what is wrong — the finding already says so. The typed taxonomy is not a richer alarm; it is the difference between an alarm that gets acted on and one that gets muted.

> Untyped drift is a pile of findings that all look the same and route nowhere. Typed drift names what broke, ranks how badly, and points at who fixes it. The typing is the capability, not the detection.

## Safe to Run Continuously

A reconciliation engine is only useful if an organization is willing to run it all the time, and that willingness depends entirely on trust that it will not do something destructive. OrgPath's engine earns that trust with two defaults.

The first is **dry-run by default**. Every scan, unless an operator explicitly promotes it for that run, computes what would change without changing anything. The output is a report and a stream of telemetry, not a set of writes. Promotion to write-mode is a deliberate, per-run decision, never the standing posture. An organization can run the engine continuously from day one, in detection-only mode, and see exactly what it would do before ever letting it do anything.

The second is **halt-on-critical**. If a scan turns up a high-severity, codebook-integrity finding — a Slot collision, the kind of thing that means canon itself is broken — the engine stops the line. It does not proceed to remediate other findings while the foundation is in question. It surfaces an escalation and waits for a human, because a substrate that auto-remediates on top of a broken codebook would propagate the breakage faster, not fix it.

Between them, these defaults make continuous reconciliation safe. The engine watches always, reports always, and acts only when an operator has chosen to let it and the foundation is sound. That combination — typed findings, dry-run default, halt-on-critical — is what no surveyed platform offers for organizational structure, because none of them treats organizational structure as a validated substrate that *can* be reconciled.

> The engine is safe to run continuously because it shows its work before doing it and stops itself when the foundation is in doubt. Detection is always on; remediation is opt-in and self-halting.

The four capabilities so far describe a substrate that is decomposed, validated, composable, and self-reconciling — within one tenant, in one cloud. The next chapter takes up the capability that none of the others imply and that Microsoft specifically cannot compose: making all of this hold across federal cloud boundaries as a single reconciled plane.
